extracted.intended_audience: students of American government and politics; municipal officials; civic reformers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for municipal functions, ownership of utilities, city planning, and county government organization and administration, aimed at explaining which arrangements are appropriate, their duties, and conditions for success. Covers legal/policy practices (franchises, home rule), institutional forms (boards, commissions), and prosecutorial and judicial roles at the county level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to provide free public baths (New York law)
rubrics_metrics.description: The law of the state of New York makes the construction of free baths obligatory upon cities with over 50,000 inhabitants and permissible for others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: New York City's municipal baths investment (circa 1908) was $3,000,000 with multiple bathing places; Boston, Chicago, Buffalo, Baltimore, Louisville operate bath-houses year-round. Purpose is to recognize personal cleanliness as part of public health and comfort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aims/objectives of municipal recreation and hygiene work
rubrics_metrics.description: Municipal work should be undertaken in light of these objects: (1) take children from streets/alleys to better play environments; (2) encourage working boys/girls and adults to spend idle hours in wholesome environments; (3) encourage personal hygiene (exercise and bathing); (4) furnish wholesome amusement for adults who do not participate in gym/athletic activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan work to attract both children and adults, hold their interest until habitual attendance is established, and use programmes/athletics/plays/games to promote bathing, skill, courage, and respect for others. (Quoted from The American City, Oct. 1909.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Municipal waterfront recreation provision
rubrics_metrics.description: Cities may attract people to waterfronts by building recreational piers above regular docks so as not to interfere with traffic, and by providing music at these places on summer evenings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: New York City built recreational piers for evening music and non-interference with commercial docks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of municipal reforms within broader economic context
rubrics_metrics.description: Municipal experiments (baths, playgrounds, etc.) do not solve fundamental urban problems, which are connected with poverty, industry, transportation, agriculture, and natural resource development — matters of economics as well as government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy and municipal reform should be linked to larger economic questions; do not treat municipal reforms as isolated remedies for deep structural problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capture of land 'unearned increment' through taxation (single-tax principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition that large annual 'unearned increment' in land values accrues to owners has led reformers to advocate diverting this money to the public treasury by taxation of land values (single tax doctrine).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocated effects include raising wages, increasing capital earnings, alleviating poverty (claims of Henry George). Practical stance: gradual increase in proportion of municipal taxation upon land rather than improvements is desirable (Professor Seager). Examples and caution: do not assume rigid single-tax application without considering objections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific city planning and planning commission duties
rubrics_metrics.description: Some states authorize municipalities to create permanent planning commissions whose duties include studying topography, parks and playgrounds, locations of public buildings, terminals and waterfronts, congestion and transportation, and kindred matters for future growth, health, comfort, employment, and standard of life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scientific planning preserves air, light, and sunshine; examples contrast broad avenues of Washington to narrow lanes of older Boston/New York. Planning commissions should use foresight and a sound public policy to secure social values created by city growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three general modes of conducting municipal utilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Present methods: (1) private ownership under public regulation; (2) public ownership with private operation (municipality leases plant to corporation with stipulated service/charge standards); (3) public ownership and operation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: waterworks of Denver and subways of Boston/New York (public ownership with private operation); water/electric-light plants sometimes publicly owned and operated. Choice of mode depends on scale, returns, and willingness of private capitalists to finance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Franchise-granting practices and regulatory constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Important franchises are increasingly made dependent on popular vote; grants are limited to shorter terms (commonly ~25 years); municipalities customarily impose close restrictions on charges/service and require compensation (services, cash payment, or annual rental) from private companies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically franchises were bestowed cheaply causing corruption; modern practice limits terms and requires municipal control over service and extensions. Example: Cleveland street railway settlement limited net earning and gave strict municipal control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on municipal ownership expansion (National Civic Federation 1907 view)
rubrics_metrics.description: Commission concluded municipal ownership should not be extended to revenue-producing industries not involving public health, safety, transportation, or permanent occupation of public streets/grounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reflects caution rooted in concerns about corruption and inefficiency in municipal management; practitioners should weigh where public ownership is appropriate and where private/regulatory arrangements suit better.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions for successful municipal ownership
rubrics_metrics.description: Municipal ownership and operation will not succeed unless high standards of civil service are established and there is a large and influential group permanently interested in economical and efficient management of the enterprise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Municipal ownership's success depends on community standards and ideals; it is neither intrinsically good nor bad. Examples show successes in some cities and corruption/inefficiency in others (e.g., Philadelphia).

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of municipal monopolies and need for public control
rubrics_metrics.description: Many municipal utilities are monopolies (competition seldom regulates prices/services); thus, absent public control, private owners could fix charges the traffic will bear (e.g., only one streetcar line on a street).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of monopoly character, public regulation or ownership is necessary to protect consumers; unrestricted private franchises historically led to corruption and exploitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of county boards and comparative advantages
rubrics_metrics.description: County boards divide into: (i) small board of three or more members elected at large or from large districts; (ii) representative board with one member elected from each township. Small boards can meet more often and be held responsible; representative boards are more representative and deliberative and present fewer collusion opportunities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both systems have been criticized as wasteful, inefficient, and sometimes corrupt; some states add other organs (e.g., Indiana's county council) to check county boards.

rubrics_metrics.name: General functions of the county board
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical functions: levy of taxes and appropriation of local funds; maintenance of roads and highways; construction and care of county buildings; relief of the poor; and control of elections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distribution of these functions varies among states (e.g., New Hampshire/Connecticut vest finance in county convention; Massachusetts vests financial power in legislature). Be aware of state-specific allocation of responsibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problems from narrow enumeration of county powers and home rule reforms
rubrics_metrics.description: When county powers are narrowly enumerated by constitution/statute, counties must seek innumerable special acts from the state legislature, destroying 'home rule' and creating legislative confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reforms like Michigan's 1908 grant of broad ordinance powers (subject to not opposing general state laws and gubernatorial veto) and California's 1911 charter provisions (boards of freeholders drafting charters, popular and legislative approval) mitigate need for special acts and enable local reorganization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements of county home rule charter (Los Angeles example, 1912)
rubrics_metrics.description: Elements include: commission form of government (board of five members) in control; board appoints county officers (except assessor, auditor, district attorney); creation of new offices (corporation counsel, purchasing agent, superintendent of charities, public defender); appointment of civil service commissioners; creation of a road commissioner with full power under board direction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Charter boards may be initiated by county board or petition; charter drafting board elected and charter requires popular and legislative approval. These elements aim to modernize county administration and centralize professional management.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection and organization of county officials and courts
rubrics_metrics.description: County officials (justice/police/finance) vary in number and powers; many offices are elective and independent; judges may be elected popularly, appointed by governor with council, or chosen by legislature; judicial organization varies — separate county judge in some states, grouped judicial districts in others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terms vary (often six to twelve years for judges). Offices and duties are frequently determined by state legislature; local variation is significant and affects administration and accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and importance of the prosecuting attorney
rubrics_metrics.description: The prosecuting attorney (district attorney) is generally elective and charged with instituting and conducting criminal prosecutions and representing the county in civil suits; may appoint assistants; salary sometimes derived from fees or fixed salary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fees can incentivize activity but may encourage useless prosecutions; the character and vigor of the prosecutor significantly affect community order and can either check corruption or enable it. High-profile prosecutions have propelled officials to higher office (examples: Deneen, Folk, Heney).

rubrics_metrics.name: Grand jury vs. prosecution by information — procedural and constitutional safeguards
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditionally the grand jury takes preliminary steps in hearing evidence and bringing indictments; prosecutors typically determine what cases come before the grand jury. Several states have authorized prosecutions on 'information' presented by the prosecutor, reducing grand jury use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substituting a single official's will for the grand jury's group judgment has grave dangers; some constitutions (e.g., Oklahoma) require preliminary examinations before felony prosecution by information to safeguard accused. Restricting grand jury increases prosecutor power — useful if used well, disastrous if abused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects of early franchise practices and public sentiment change
rubrics_metrics.description: Early state legislatures often granted almost priceless public privileges (franchises) without restrictions, leading to corruption; in the last decade (circa text) public sentiment has awakened against free exploitation of municipal monopolies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modern trend is toward greater regulation, shorter franchise terms, requiring compensation and municipal control — reforms intended to reduce corruption and protect public interest.
